criteria.criterion: The change description names the root cause (owner priority from addenda is not an input to plan ordering and the order is never checked against it) and the fix sits in crates/athena-core/src/plan.rs, not in one job's request.
criteria.evidence: I read the diff. The CHANGELOG entry gives the root cause: "a priority stated in a BRIEF.md addendum was never an input to plan ordering ... and nothing compared the built order with the priorities". The candidate commit message is only the placeholder "candidate", so the CHANGELOG entry is the change description. The fix is at plan construction and is general, with no job ids. `BriefTopic` gains `priority` (reading.rs `addendum_priority`). `plan_entry` raises an entry to the priority of the addendum it serves. plan.rs adds `Plan::priority_violations`, and drain.rs calls it on every built plan. The real BRIEF.md addendum "2026-10-25: Speed first" says "ranks above all other work", and `addendum_priority` reads that as High, so the fix covers the owner's actual addendum.

criteria.criterion: Run `cargo test -p athena-core plan`: a new test builds a plan where an addendum-stated top priority belongs to a newer, later-rung item and asserts it is in the first wave. The same test fails when the change is reverted.
criteria.evidence: `reading::tests::an_addendum_priority_puts_the_work_serving_it_in_the_first_plan_wave ... ok` (51 passed). In the test, the newest entry "new" is on the Implementation rung and the two older entries are on OwnerGoals. "new" serves an addendum that says `Priority: urgent`. The test asserts `plan.groups[0] == ["new"]` and that no violations are reported. I reasoned about a revert from the code and did not run one, because the verifier may not change files. If the non-test change is reverted, `BriefTopic.priority` no longer exists and the test does not compile. Without the raise in `plan_entry`, `entries[2].priority` stays Normal and the lower rung puts "new" last, so the asserts fail.

criteria.criterion: Run `cargo test -p athena-core plan`: a new test asserts the order check reports a plan whose top-priority item is not first, and passes a correctly ordered plan. It covers the general case with several items, not one job's ids.
criteria.evidence: `plan::tests::the_order_check_flags_a_plan_that_puts_a_lower_priority_item_first ... ok`. The test uses five generic items a–e with low, urgent and high priorities plus a dependency. The order from `build` passes the check. A hand-made age order is flagged for `c (urgent)` and for `b (high)`; b is high because high-priority d depends on it. Two items of equal priority in swapped order are not flagged.

criteria.criterion: Run `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --all-targets` and `cargo test`: all pass, with the existing plan ordering tests (dependencies first, effective priority) unchanged.
criteria.evidence: Athena's recorded checks show that fmt, clippy (-D warnings) and `cargo test --locked` (1456 tests) passed on this tree. In the diff, the plan.rs test module only gains the new test. The existing tests (`dependencies_win_over_priority_and_pull_their_prerequisites_forward`, `urgent_comes_before_high_before_normal_and_a_dependency_still_comes_first`, and others) are unedited and pass in my targeted run. The effective-priority fixpoint was moved into `effective_priorities` with the same logic.

criteria.criterion: CHANGELOG.md has an entry that states the cause and the new check, for an outside reader.
criteria.evidence: I read CHANGELOG.md. A new entry under Added gives the cause and the new input: an addendum `Priority:` line, or wording such as "ranks above all other work" or "top priority". It also names the check, `Plan::priority_violations`, and says `athena drain` prints each violation it finds as a note.

findings.summary: The drain wiring of the order check has no test
findings.evidence: The diff adds a note for each violation in drain.rs but does not change crates/athena-cli/tests/drain.rs, although that file is in the deliverables. `Plan::build` always follows priority, so in practice this note fires only if `build` regresses. Nothing tests that the note appears.

findings.summary: An addendum's priority overrides a lower `Priority:` line in the request itself
findings.evidence: The raise is skipped only when `job.priorities` (the `athena priority` records) is non-empty. A request whose own text says `Priority: low` but that matches an urgent or high addendum is raised anyway. That request line is also an explicit owner statement. The CHANGELOG mentions only the record as being left alone.

findings.summary: Priority wording is matched by substring, so a negation still counts
findings.evidence: `lower.contains("top priority")` also matches text such as "this is not a top priority" and makes the addendum High. Requests are matched to addenda by shared words (at least 2), so a wrong match could raise unrelated work.

summary: The change passes: all five acceptance criteria are met, and no finding is a blocker or major. It fixes the cause where it starts, in planning. A priority stated in a BRIEF.md addendum is now read: an addendum with a `Priority: <level>` line, or text saying its work "ranks above all other work" or is a "top priority", carries that priority. `plan_entry` raises any request that serves that addendum to at least that priority, unless the job has an `athena priority` record. `Plan::priority_violations` checks a built order and lists every item planned after one of lower priority, and `athena drain` prints each as a note. The real "Speed first" addendum in BRIEF.md uses the "ranks above all other work" wording, so the fix applies to the owner's actual case. I ran `cargo test -p athena-core plan` and all 51 tests passed, including the two new ones. The first new test shows a newer, lower-rung item serving an urgent addendum landing alone in the first wave. The second shows the check flagging a bad five-item order and passing a correct one. For fmt, clippy and the full test suite I relied on Athena's recorded passing runs. Reverting the fix would make the new test fail; I worked that out from the code and did not run a revert, because I may not change files. The existing ordering tests are untouched. There are three minor issues: the drain note has no test, an addendum's priority overrides a lower `Priority:` line in the request itself, and the wording match counts negated phrases such as "not a top priority". All four changed files are on the deliverables list.
